Why your site is invisible to ChatGPT (and how to check in 30 seconds)

August 2026

Someone asks ChatGPT for a recommendation. Your kind of business. Your city. Your exact service.

ChatGPT thinks for a moment. Then it lists three competitors. Not you.

Not because they're better. Not because ChatGPT has an opinion. Because it literally cannot see your website.

This isn't hypothetical. We checked.

What we found when we audited real websites

We built ReportReady to answer one question: can AI search engines actually see your site?

We ran audits on dozens of websites. SaaS companies. Agencies. Well-known tools. The results surprised us.

More than half the sites we checked were invisible to ChatGPT and Gemini.

Including Calendly. Notion. Figma.

And including our own site. We built the audit tool and we still failed our own audit.

Our own site failed. Here's what happened.

When we first ran ReportReady against getreportready.com, this is what came back:

  • SEO: 70 out of 100
  • AI Readiness: 50 out of 100

Two high-severity issues:

  1. No Schema Markup on the homepage. Schema markup is structured data that tells AI crawlers what your site is about. Without it, ChatGPT doesn't know if you're a business, a person, a product, or a blog post.
  2. No meta description. When someone searches for what you do, AI has no summary of your site to show them. You don't appear in results because the AI doesn't have enough information to include you.

We fixed both issues. It took 30 minutes. Now our site scores 100 out of 100 across all four categories: SEO, Performance, Accessibility, and AI Readiness.

If the people who built the audit tool missed these problems, it's reasonable to assume most websites have them too. And they do.

Why this happens

AI crawlers work differently from Google's crawler. Most sites are built with Google SEO in mind. Keywords, backlinks, page speed. That stuff still matters, but AI search engines look at different signals.

Here are the three most common reasons sites are invisible to AI:

1. AI crawlers are blocked in robots.txt

Your robots.txt file tells crawlers which parts of your site they can access. Many sites block AI-specific crawlers like GPTBot (ChatGPT), Google-Extended (Gemini), or PerplexityBot without realizing it. Sometimes a developer added these blocks years ago. Sometimes a plugin added them automatically. Either way, the result is the same: AI search engines literally cannot read your site.

2. No structured data (Schema Markup)

Google can figure out what a page is about from keywords and context. AI crawlers rely much more heavily on structured data. Schema markup tells them explicitly: "This is a software product. It costs $99 per month. It has a 14-day free trial." Without it, the AI has to guess. And it usually guesses wrong, or skips you entirely.

3. Missing or weak meta descriptions

When ChatGPT or Gemini returns search results, it pulls from your meta description. No description means no summary. No summary means no listing. It's that simple.

What happens if you don't fix it

AI search usage is growing fast. ChatGPT alone has over 400 million weekly active users. Gemini is built into every Android phone. Perplexity is growing faster than any search engine in history.

Every day your site is invisible to these platforms, you're losing traffic to competitors who fixed this six months ago.

The fix is usually straightforward. Add a meta description tag. Add a JSON-LD schema block to your homepage. Check your robots.txt for AI crawler blocks. A competent developer can do all three in an afternoon.

But you can't fix what you don't know is broken. And most people don't know.

Nobody goes looking for a problem that doesn't announce itself. Your site loads fine. It ranks on Google. Everything looks normal. But behind the scenes, AI search engines are skipping you entirely. You only find out when a client asks "why don't you show up in ChatGPT?" and you don't have an answer.
